opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think retrieval-augmented generation is going to stay important for a long time, and the reasons go beyond the usual "it reduces hallucinations" argument.

In an enterprise setting, and certainly in finance where I spend most of my time, the value of a system usually isn't what the model memorized during pretraining. It's whether the system can work with information that is proprietary, very recent, or changing constantly. A model trained months ago doesn't know about this morning's earnings release, an internal policy document, or a client's specific portfolio. Retrieval is the most practical way to connect a general-purpose model to that kind of information without retraining every time something changes.

The second reason is attribution and trust. If you're making decisions with real consequences, you need to know where an answer came from. A well-designed RAG system lets you point back to the source document, so a user can check the claim and an auditor can reconstruct why the system said what it said. That traceability matters a lot in regulated industries, and you can't get it from a model answering out of its parameters.

Third, retrieval gives you a control surface. You can decide which documents a given user may see, enforce entitlements, remove outdated or problematic content, and update the knowledge base without touching the model. From a governance and safety standpoint that's very attractive.

That said, I don't want to suggest RAG is a solved problem or a cure-all. A lot of the failures we see happen in the retrieval step. The system pulls the wrong document, an incomplete one, or a stale version, and the model then answers fluently and confidently from bad context. There's also evidence that adding retrieval can change a model's safety behavior in ways people don't expect. Systems that behave well on their own can become more willing to produce problematic outputs when given retrieved context. So you can't assume the safety properties of the base model carry over to the full pipeline. You have to evaluate the system as it's actually deployed, with your own data and your own risks.

So my view is that RAG remains essential, but it should be treated as a system-engineering and evaluation problem, not a bolt-on feature. Longer context windows and better agents don't remove the need to ground answers in the right, authorized, current information. If anything they raise the stakes for doing retrieval well.

r002.rationale: It says a well-designed RAG system can point back to a source document, but does not state that attributing an answer to a source requires retrieving that source.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that RAG has turned out to be much more durable than a lot of people predicted a couple of years ago. There was this narrative that as context windows got longer and models got better at memorizing, retrieval would just become a stopgap we'd eventually throw away. And in practice the opposite has happened. It's become more central, not less, and I think that's because the hard problems in enterprise AI were never really about whether the model could fit the information in context. They were about which information, from where, under whose permissions, and whether you can trace an answer back to its source.

So I tend to think about RAG less as a technique and more as the interface between a model and an organization's actual knowledge. Enterprises don't have a static corpus. They have documents that change daily, policies that get superseded, data that's segmented by region or business unit or regulatory regime. You simply cannot bake that into weights, and even if you could, you wouldn't want to, because then every update becomes a retraining event and every access-control question becomes a nightmare. Retrieval keeps the knowledge outside the model, where it can be versioned, audited, and governed with the tooling companies already have.

The second piece, which I care about a lot from an evaluation perspective, is grounding and attribution. If a model gives you an answer in a financial or legal or healthcare setting, the question isn't just "is this correct," it's "can you show me why." Retrieval gives you a natural mechanism for that. You can point to the passage. And that changes how you evaluate the system, because now you can decompose the problem: did we retrieve the right thing, and given what we retrieved, did the model use it faithfully? Those are two different failure modes with two different fixes, and separating them is enormously valuable when you're trying to improve a production system rather than just a benchmark score.

What has changed, I'd say, is what we mean by RAG. The early version was embed some chunks, do a nearest-neighbor lookup, stuff the top five into the prompt. That's a very thin notion of retrieval. What we're seeing now is much richer: hybrid search, query rewriting, retrieval over structured data and tools alongside text, multi-step retrieval where the model decides it needs more and goes back. In agentic systems, retrieval is just one of the actions an agent can take, and it's often the most important one. So the term survives, but the architecture underneath it has gotten considerably more sophisticated.

And then there's the pragmatic reality that enterprises are cost-sensitive and latency-sensitive. Shoving a million tokens into context for every query is expensive and slow, and it degrades quality in ways that are hard to predict. Good retrieval is a form of focus. It's deciding what the model should pay attention to, and I think that remains a fundamentally good idea regardless of how capable the underlying models become.

r001.rationale: It says retrieval is an important action in agentic systems, but does not identify many AI agents as RAG systems.

r002.rationale: It links grounding and attribution to retrieval, explaining that retrieval lets you point to the passage supporting an answer.

r003.rationale: It separates finding relevant information from using it faithfully, but does not say retrieval turns an open-ended question into extracting an answer from a document.

astra-6.text:
I think retrieval remains really important because enterprise knowledge is constantly changing. Even if a model has a very large context window or knows a lot from pretraining, it doesn’t automatically have access to the latest internal documentation, or know which information a particular employee is allowed to see.

Retrieval gives you a way to connect the model to that information at the time of a request. It also gives you something to inspect: which documents did we retrieve, and does the answer actually follow from them? That’s useful both for building trust and for diagnosing failures.

But retrieval doesn’t automatically make an answer correct. You can retrieve an outdated document, miss the relevant passage, or have the model misinterpret what it finds. So I think the continuing importance of RAG is as part of a broader system—one that manages access, keeps information current, and evaluates retrieval quality alongside answer quality. Better models help, but they don’t eliminate those requirements.

sol-6.1.text:
I think retrieval continues to be important because so much of what an enterprise needs a model to know lives outside the model. It’s internal documentation, information that changes frequently, or information that only certain people should have access to. Even a very capable model needs a way to connect to that information at the time you ask a question.

And the value isn’t just getting the right facts into the prompt. It’s also being able to show where an answer came from. If you’re using a system to make a business decision, you want to be able to inspect the underlying source and understand whether it supports the answer.

Of course, retrieval doesn’t automatically solve that problem. You can retrieve the wrong document, miss an important piece of context, or generate an answer that isn’t supported by what you retrieved. So you need to evaluate the whole system, including whether it can recognize when it doesn’t have enough information. But that connection between a model and an organization’s current, permissioned knowledge remains very useful as models improve.
